title: Onprem / Air-gapped runtime performance deep dive
summary: SE-led deep dive on on-prem air-gapped deployment requirements and runtime perf tuning. Discussed artifact delivery (images/tarball checksums), offline license activation, GPU driver and CUDA dependencies, recommended quantization profiles and batching strategy to meet 100ms token latency SLO for 1k TPS workloads, and KV cache persistence options. Action items include sharing offline licensing guide and a benchmark plan.
next_steps: Redwood to share offline artifact delivery checklist and signed-off checksum files (S3 pre-signed for transfer) by 2025-05-09
Run initial on-prem benchmark with Acme sample workload - Redwood SE to provide benchmark script and Docker image sha256 - target run week of 2025-05-12
Customer to provide GPU node specs and network topology (air-gap details/NFS availability) by 2025-05-08
Schedule follow-up pilot planning call with infra and security (2 weeks out)
action_items: Ravi Patel (Redwood SE) - Share offline licensing proposal and activation flow (file-based license + HSM integration notes) - due 2025-05-09
Maya Chen (Redwood AE) - Send pricing/committed capacity worksheet and pilot engagement SOW - due 2025-05-12
Carlos Rivera (Acme) - Provide GPU driver version constraints and whether CUDA 12 is allowed in their air-gapped environment - due 2025-05-08
Priya Shah (Acme) - Confirm whether NFS or object-store with gateway will be used for artifact hosting inside air-gap - due 2025-05-08
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-06 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lina Ortiz (Redwood SE), James Holloway (CTO - Acme), Priya Shah (Platform Eng), Carlos Rivera (ML Infra), Mei Lin (Security)
---
00:00 Speaker 1 (Maya): hey everyone thanks for joining today we're gonna focus on the on prem air gap runtime perf stuff and artifact delivery checklists, i'll hand it to ravi to kick off with the topology assumptions
00:18 Speaker 2 (Ravi): thanks maya, yeah hi all, quick call out on assumptions: we assume acme has at least one GPU cluster behind an air-gapped jumpbox, images can be transferred via physical media or pre-staged tarballs, there's a local package registry or object store; if not we recommended an appliance pattern. does that match what you have?
00:34 Speaker 3 (James): yes that's mostly right, we have 8x A100 80GB on two nodes, isolated network, we do have an internal objectstore (s3-compatible) but it's also air-gapped; we can't pull from internet.
00:45 Speaker 2 (Ravi): perfect. okay i'll go through deliverables: we provide signed artifact bundles (docker images as tarballs + model weights as shards), sha256 checksums, and an offline license file. For the runtime we have two flavors - a container runtime for standard on-prem and an rpm/deb install for appliance-only installs. In air-gap we recommend the tarball flow.
01:06 Speaker 4 (Priya): question: driver versions - are you tied to a specific CUDA/cuDNN? our infra team standardizes on CUDA11.8 right now, we haven't standardized CUDA12 yet.
01:18 Speaker 2 (Ravi): good question. our latest runtime builds are validated on CUDA 11.8 and 12.1; for A100 we prefer CUDA 11.8 with cuDNN 8.x in our tests, but we can provide back-compat instructions. if you can't upgrade to 12 we can still provide images, but performance/quantization runtime paths may vary slightly.
01:36 Speaker 5 (Mei): from security we need to understand the offline licensing activation flow. we can't have a service phone-home.
01:44 Speaker 2 (Ravi): absolutely - offline activation is file-based: we issue a license blob tied to a hardware id or customer-provided activation token. Activation can happen via an HSM/KMS inside the airgap or by co-locating a license manager VM. we document signature verification steps and key rotation guidance. we'll share the exact flow.
02:05 Speaker 3 (Carlos): what about driver packaging? we usually do not allow vendor drivers to be installed without approval - can you provide vendor-approved driver patches or a specific driver bundle?
02:17 Speaker 2 (Ravi): we can provide driver compatibility matrix and recommend exact NVIDIA driver versions. normally we don't ship drivers due to licensing, but we can package a driver installer wrapper that references your internal repo. we'll include checksums.
02:31 Speaker 1 (Maya): let's pivot to runtime perf - latency and throughput. acme mentioned wanting ~100ms per token median latency for interactive app and also support bursts to 1k concurrent request within 200ms p95, can you elaborate on that?
02:48 Speaker 3 (James): yes that's what product wants. right now on hosted we see lower latencies but we need the air-gapped deployment to match for regulatory reasons.
02:56 Speaker 2 (Ravi): ok so few levers: model quantization (int8, q4_0, q4_1 profiles), batching sizes, prefix/KV cache, and kernel selection. for short-sequence interactive use we recommend aggressive KV caching and small dynamic batching. i'll share some numbers: on A100 80GB with q4_1 we saw ~60-90ms per token at batch size 1 with optimized kernels and kv cache warm, throughput at batch 8 jumps to ~400 tokens/sec per GPU but with higher tail latency.
03:25 Speaker 4 (Priya): can you explain kv cache persistence - if we warm cache once is it stored to disk between restarts or is it ephemeral?
03:33 Speaker 2 (Ravi): currently the KV cache is in-memory per runtime process; we offer optional periodic snapshotting of cold prefixes to disk - it's not automatic in every build but we do have a persisting module in our enterprise runtime that will serialize commonly accessed KV pages to local SSD with LRU eviction. in air-gap we recommend enabling that to reduce cold-start token cost.
03:57 Speaker 5 (Mei): does that introduce PII risk? if prefixes are stored, we need encryption at rest and audit logs.
04:06 Speaker 2 (Ravi): yes, snapshot files are encrypted with a customer-provided key via KMS/HSM integration. we also log access events. we'll include the audit log format in the security docs.
04:18 Speaker 1 (Maya): rought numbers: can you give an example run for a 2k token prompt with batching?
04:25 Speaker 2 (Ravi): sure - for a 2k prompt using q4_1 on A100, single-stream latency from token 1 to last token is dominated by forward pass and kv application. with batch size 1 and optimized kernels we saw ~2.5-3.0 seconds end-to-end for 2k request; with batching (batch 4) throughput increases substantially but latency per request increases - so for interactive use we lean batch size 1-2 and KV caching.
04:50 Speaker 3 (James): what about CPU / host memory requirements? we can't starve the host.
04:55 Speaker 2 (Ravi): host needs enough RAM for kernel workspace and kv cache - we recommend 256GB host RAM for 80GB A100 nodes if you expect heavy concurrent contexts; that prevents swapping. Also use nvme local SSD for checkpoint/snapshot.
05:10 Speaker 4 (Priya): network - will the runtime try to access internet for telemetry? we need total air-gap.
05:15 Speaker 2 (Ravi): no phone-home in air-gap deploy. we build a variant that disables telemetry and auto-update. logs are written locally and you can configure a secure pull to the Redwood console via an approved landing zone if desired.
05:28 Speaker 1 (Maya): good. let's dig into quantization - we mentioned q4_0 vs q4_1 and int8. what's the tradeoff?
05:36 Speaker 2 (Ravi): q4_0 is faster and smaller but less numerically stable; q4_1 gives better quality at a small perf hit. int8 can outperform both on speed if the model is calibrated but requires more validation for hallucination/regression. typical path: start with q4_1 for production, run evals, move to int8 for cost sensitive workloads after regression tests.
05:58 Speaker 3 (James): how do you handle kernel selection? sometimes the default GEMM kernels are not optimal for long sequences.
06:06 Speaker 2 (Ravi): our runtime has a kernel selector that picks between cuBLAS, CUTLASS and custom fused kernels based on model shape and sequence length. we auto-benchmark during build; for long sequences we'll switch to blocked attention kernels to reduce memory blowup. we can also provide a config override if you want to force a kernel for predictable latency.
06:25 Speaker 4 (Priya): batching - how does dynamic batching affect p95? do you support adaptive batching?
06:32 Speaker 2 (Ravi): yes we support adaptive batching with max latency SLO caps. you configure a max latency target (e.g., 120ms) and the runtime will aggregate up to the batch size while respecting the SLO. this reduces token-cost by increasing GPU utilization. note tail latencies can still spike for large model steps; we also support per-route policies and can route latency-sensitive requests to a lower batch domain (dedicated pool).
06:56 Speaker 1 (Maya): are there recommendations for autoscaling in air-gap?
07:00 Speaker 2 (Ravi): autoscaling in pure air-gap is typically node-level via your cluster autoscaler or manual; we provide an autoscaler agent that works with offline metrics. for capacity bursts we recommend a mixed pool model: small low-latency pool and a larger high-throughput pool for batch workloads. you can set cross-fallback rules.
07:18 Speaker 3 (Carlos): offline artifact delivery - what's the expected format and what checks do you require?
07:24 Speaker 2 (Ravi): we deliver artifacts as gzipped tarballs: runtime.tar.gz, models.tar.gz (sharded weights), license.blob, checksums.txt (sha256), and an install manifest. for extra security we sign the manifest with our private key and include the public key for verification. transfer options: secure USB, SFTP over jumpbox, or pre-stage to your acceptance S3.
07:44 Speaker 5 (Mei): can we verify signatures offline? we need a deterministic verification flow.
07:50 Speaker 2 (Ravi): yes, we include an openssl s_signature and a verification script; instructions are in the offline checklist. verification is fully offline.
07:59 Speaker 4 (Priya): are there licensing limits based on node counts or GPU counts?
08:04 Speaker 1 (Maya): we typically license per-GPU or per-reserved-capacity unit depending on the contract; offline activations will include the allowed device id list. if you have ephemeral nodes we also support floating licenses via a token server inside the airgap.
08:20 Speaker 3 (James): regarding benchmarking - what workload should we run to get meaningful latency/throughput?
08:27 Speaker 2 (Ravi): we'll provide a benchmark harness: payloads that reflect your interactive prompts and batch inference tests. it includes warm-up, kv priming steps, and load profiles. we recommend doing both cold-start and warm cache runs, and run p95/p50 metrics. we'll give you a script that emits per-token timings.
08:46 Speaker 4 (Priya): are there any filesystem permissions concerns for storing KV snapshots?
08:51 Speaker 2 (Ravi): snapshots are regular files, we recommend mounting to a dedicated path with restrictive perms, encrypted fs (dm-crypt) or LUKS, and the runtime runs as non-root. we'll include an SELinux policy example.
09:05 Speaker 3 (Carlos): curious about memory management - do you use offload (cpu/gpu split) for very large contexts?
09:12 Speaker 2 (Ravi): yes, we support KV offload to CPU and NVMe - hybrid sharding. for extremely long contexts we will spill LRU pages to NVMe. performance depends on PCIe bandwidth; on machines with PCIe Gen4 NVMe we saw acceptable latencies but recommend keeping hot prefixes in GPU memory.
09:34 Speaker 1 (Maya): any known issues with multi-GPU coordination?
09:37 Speaker 2 (Ravi): in multi-GPU mode we use tensor parallelism and chunked kv replication; synchronization can add ~3-8ms depending on NCCL and interconnect. on DGX-like setups with NVSwitch it's minimal. we'll provide NCCL and driver tuning tips.
09:52 Speaker 3 (James): security again - audit logs for inference requests - do you capture payloads?
09:58 Speaker 5 (Mei): ideally no raw PII; we need token-level metrics but not full prompt storage unless customer opts in and encryption is used.
10:06 Speaker 2 (Ravi): by default we capture metrics and hashes; storing raw prompts is opt-in and can be redacted. all logs can be forwarded to your SIEM; we support syslog and file export.
10:18 Speaker 1 (Maya): ok let's talk about concrete perf numbers we can include in the pilot. Ravi can you outline a recommended pilot sizing and expected throughput targets?
10:26 Speaker 2 (Ravi): recommended pilot: 2 A100 nodes (8 GPUs total) for interactive evaluation with a mix of 1k small prompt QPS and periodic 2k token requests. with q4_1 and kv warm, expect ~600-800 tokens/sec per GPU sustained for mixed workload, median token latency ~80-120ms; p95 depends on batching and concurrency but should be under 200-250ms with the low-latency pool. we'll include explicit benchmark templates.
10:52 Speaker 4 (Priya): if we can't match host RAM recommendations, what's the graceful degradation?
10:56 Speaker 2 (Ravi): you'll see increased swap and higher tail latencies; we can enforce resident set limits and reduce batch sizes and sequence lengths to mitigate. also enabling KV snapshotting helps reduce memory pressure by offloading cold keys.
11:12 Speaker 3 (Carlos): can you support offline model quantization tooling or do we need to run quantization inside our network?
11:18 Speaker 2 (Ravi): we can provide quantized artifacts as part of the artifact bundle if you allow us to produce them pre-shipping; otherwise we ship the quantization toolchain so you can run it internally. for air-gap often teams want artifacts pre-quantized to avoid on-prem builds.
11:33 Speaker 1 (Maya): Lina, do you want to add anything on artifact integrity?
11:36 Speaker 4 (Lina): yeah we also recommend signing each shard and providing a manifest that lists file sizes and checksums; use reproducible tar flags to avoid timestamp churn. we also include a verification script that will failfast if checksums don't match.
11:48 Speaker 5 (Mei): network egress - if we later want to push telemetry out through a controlled jump host what protocols would you use?
11:55 Speaker 2 (Ravi): we use HTTPS with mutual TLS and token-based auth. the telemetry agent can be configured to batch and push on schedule. all configs are offline-editable.
12:07 Speaker 1 (Maya): ok good. wrapping up - next steps and action items summarized shortly. any other blockers?
12:13 Speaker 3 (James): none immediate. Carlos will check driver policy, Priya will confirm artifact hosting inside the airgap.
12:20 Speaker 1 (Maya): great thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and the benchmark harness.
---
Meeting end.
notes: Provided options for driver handling: compatibility matrix + wrapper installer, not shipping drivers by default
KV cache snapshotting recommended for warm latency; persisted snapshots encrypted with customer keys
